judgments.reasoning: Read captions 0–220s and catalogue chapters Introduction, Filtering a table, and Using VLOOKUP. At 18.89s a fresh salesperson-table example begins; use 19s rather than including the preceding introduction fragment at 18s. At 78.54–96.84s the narrator explains finding Jonathan and returning corresponding sales; at 119.28–155.67s he selects B4:E16, counts sales as column 3 with salesperson in column 1, and chooses FALSE for exact matching. The answer is completed at 181.83–187.65s before changing the lookup. Confirm f1/f3 only: the sorting passage does not identify the first column, so it is not full f4 coverage. The 'most business cases ... always be false' phrasing at 157.95–170.31s is overbroad practical advice, not the operative match rule; the actual example explicitly requires exact matching. The worksheet zoom, selection, formula entry and returned value are strong spreadsheet-demo cues, though frames were not inspected. No conditional/error-handling knowledge is needed in this cut. Caption timing puts the result/next-example transition near 187s; keep this endpoint rather than including the next workflow.

Read 118–357s, including catalogue chapters customer master list, exact versus approximate matching and expanding the table array. Start at 151s, at the new customer-list setup (150.59s), not the preceding 'see that in a second.' At 181.11–218.29s Kim West/G5 is matched in the left-hand column and customer ID returned from column 2. At 231.38–268.42s omission defaults to TRUE, the lookup-value column is explicitly identified as unsorted, and sorting corrects the illustrated result. At 276.35–292.98s FALSE/zero is entered and two keys are checked. At 292.98–327.31s the company-column example completes the requirement to include both lookup and return columns in one table array. Thus f1/f3/f4 are taught, but not XLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH. Sorting is necessary for approximate lookup, not sufficient for exact-match semantics; the clip's observed sorted example is not a claim that every sorted approximate lookup is exact. End at 327s before completing reports and range-fixing. Selection, sorting and returned results provide concrete spreadsheet visual cues; no blocked IFERROR knowledge is used.

Read 4–221s and chapters IF Syntax, IF Formula Example and Outro. The tutorial names IF at 7s and explicitly states its logical-test/true-result/false-result syntax at 30.36–43.24s. The example establishes units greater than five, 10% of total for true, otherwise 5% (64.2–85.08s), then constructs both branches and demonstrates the result changing when units become six (114.76–178.68s). This confirms f1, not nested IF or IFS. The proposal's 187s end is too early: 'automatically copies it' is followed by 'down' in the caption beginning 187.8s. Extend to 189s to finish the copy-down action; only a brief outro transition remains, not another example. Cell G2, formula completion, recalculation and the fill handle support spreadsheet-demo visual value. The example uses already allowed multiplication/cell references and no blocked concept.

Read 5–164s and the setting-the-scene/give-room-for-feedback chapters. At 24.34–43.66s the narrator defines inspection/adaptation and identifies team, Product Owner and real end users. At 51.32–79.25s he establishes the work-order/table-component example, so the inserted review demonstration has its own context. At 86.68–99.36s he identifies the Product Owner's missing space for feedback, and at 114.41–129.91s states that a demo is only the beginning and triggers feedback. That teaches f1, not acceptance-criteria comparison. End before the distinct developer-context section at 131s. The real-meeting/example chapter structure and commentary on the demonstration support visual teaching beyond a generic talking head; caption gaps limit verification of untranscribed meeting dialogue, so no facts are inferred from those gaps. Mentioning the increment does not require the later Definition of Done concept.

Read 5–163s and Introduction/The Problem/Preparation chapters. At 12.66–23.58s the purpose is inspection of the sprint outcome and future adaptations. At 23.58–44.16s the narrator contrasts a collaborative working session with one-way demo/listing; at 81.54–110.34s he discusses inviting relevant stakeholders and telling them the work to inspect. The final working-session reminder is NOT complete at 128s: 'not limited' continues with 'to a demo and/or presentation' in the 124.98–131.46s caption. Extend to 132s to preserve this fact before feature-station setup. Confirm only f1. This is a genuinely conceptual facilitation explanation with an unusually clear purpose/anti-pattern/preparation sequence; visual support is less directly evidenced than the tool demos, but even a talking-head rendition would meet the conceptual exception. No later retrospective or Definition of Done knowledge is needed.

Read 22–234s and Problem Solving Example/Limitations/Ask Why chapters. At 57.44s a fresh coolant-on-floor problem is established. At 114–157.44s the narration chains coolant to leaking machine to leaky seal and stresses that replacing a symptom can allow recurrence. At 161.2–170.56s it explicitly says the chain can take more or fewer than five questions, confirming f3 as well as f1. The following 'almost always'/'most likely' language is an overconfident heuristic, so it should not be repeated as a guarantee. The final guard-over-screen outcome continues through the 196.8–201.6s caption; use 200s, just at the 199.84s benefits transition, to finish 'over the screen' instead of the original 199s. Recording the causal answers is not narrated, so f2 remains unconfirmed. References to the screen, shavings and dropped parts imply an on-screen causal illustration, but several causal links are visual-only and cannot be independently confirmed from captions. This is a self-contained conceptual/example segment, not a need for later fishbone knowledge.

Read the complete 0–200s transcript and the problem-solving-method, point-of-occurrence and countermeasure chapters. The opening names Five Whys/causal chains and explains observing work and getting facts. At 91.59–100.26s 'sometimes three, sometimes eight' explicitly rejects a mandatory count. At 103.59–168.15s the machine-stop chain is narrated through blown fuse, overload, insufficient lubrication, pump failure, worn shaft and absent strainer; at 172.53–183.81s the narrator checks the therefore-chain upward and applies a strainer countermeasure. The concluding distinction between symptom band-aids and root-cause solving continues into the caption at 192.9s; end at 195s, before the farewell at 194.73s becomes substantive. Confirm f1/f3, not f2's written-answer workflow. The funnel and reversible causal-chain walkthrough provide diagram/whiteboard cues, not just unsupported mention of a method. No blocked knowledge is required.

Read 148–435s and Fact tables explained/Dimension tables explained/Facts vs dimensions chapters. The initial 'is that?' finishes a question from 179s, but the immediate 'A fact table stores business events, transactions, or activity' at 181.52s is a self-sufficient definition, not an unresolved example dependency. The fresh sales table at 193.24s records events, IDs linking other tables, dates, quantities and amounts (203.36–253.12s), confirming f3. At 261.04–298.08s a separate product table describes entities/attributes; at 355.52–396.8s the facts-versus-descriptive-context contrast confirms f1. Dimension key uniqueness is not explained, so f2 is not confirmed; consistent fact grain/cardinality are also absent. End before connecting the model at 404.76s. References to table rows, IDs and the side-by-side comparison support data-table visual value. General discussion of grouping/filtering labels is understandable from earlier SQL and does not require the later Power BI relationship configuration concept. The tiny carried-over opening question is an advisory editing blemish, not a hard context failure.

Read 0–235s and What is Star Schema/Table relationships chapters. Start at 21s at the independent Awesome Chocolates example (20.96s). At 37.52–76.88s the sales-observation table is distinguished from information not present there; at 82–116s salesperson team, product attributes and geography region come from separate descriptive tables. At 127.76–165.68s the narrator draws connecting threads, and at 173.6–202.4s identifies a central sales table with surrounding business-entity tables as the star. This teaches f1 only; names used to connect the illustration do not establish unique dimension keys or one-to-many cardinality. End before the snowflake example at 205.36s: its separate targets-table argument is not necessary to understand the chosen cut and is not approved. Printed rows and drawn threads strongly imply a visual data-model explanation. No later Power BI relationship-editing or DAX mechanics are used.

Read 97–273s and Why Power BI Blocks the Loop/Handle Inactive Relationships chapters. At 133.76–167.04s the customer/store/sales example does illustrate filters taking different routes. But at 186.08–193.6s it states that Power BI forces 'only ... one direction, one path between two tables,' and at 236.96–241.6s again equates the loop/different options with a prohibited ambiguity. The approved Microsoft create-and-manage-relationships source, opened independently at its Cross filter direction discussion, permits Both and explains that loops CAN create ambiguity depending on filter configuration, not that every loop or multiple path is prohibited. This overgeneralization is part of the explanation's organizing mechanism, not a passing later-topic mention. A shorter cut stopping at 185s would still leave the example's assumed path conflict without the cross-filter configuration or a completed resolution, and would not fully teach the claimed f1's multi-table visual use. Reject rather than confirm f1 as fully taught. The table/route pointers suggest useful visuals and no blocked DAX appears inside the proposed range, but neither cures the technical rule.

Read 610–877s and Insert Chart with Slicer/Insert Tables with Quick Measures chapters. At 641.47–665.18s the new thought explains selecting sales/category fields, automatically creating a column chart, then choosing a clustered bar chart from Visualizations. At 692.29–739.37s it distinguishes changing the selected visual from clicking away to create a new slicer and selects Year from the date hierarchy. At 769.16–840.32s selection updates the chart and the narrator adjusts titles/axes/colors. This confirms f2's workflow, not the service-dashboard distinction or full audience/design facts. The imported model is an allowed prerequisite, and the range does not require knowing DAX to follow the year slicer. End at 844s before the year-over-year/year-to-date quick-measure task at 844.26s, which would require blocked measures knowledge. Older pane/interface labels merit a learner-facing version note, not a fabricated current UI claim. The narrated clicks, canvas placement and changing chart provide strong screen-demo cues.

Read 898–1127s and Column chart/Sorting chapters. The thought beginning 933.21s sets a standalone people-by-department task. At 946.77–979.41s a chart is added, Department placed on axis and Name counted as the value; at 1017.6–1033.74s sorting is changed. At 1052.14–1087.9s a second visual is created by selecting Gender and counting names. These actions confirm f2, not report-versus-dashboard or full design-rule coverage. Tighten the end to 1090s, after the male/female result and before 'there is a blank item' at 1090.96s launches an unfinished data-quality problem; the proposed 1096s stops in its introduction. The statement at 1008.45–1012.95s that default sorting is 'always' by column/bar size is overbroad and should not be promoted as a general rule. The meaningful demo actions are correct and visual. Earlier imported employee data is allowed; implicit counting is explained and does not require the later DAX-measures concept.

Read 800–962s and the catalogue's UI-walkthrough-to-Bins boundary. The proposed 837s starts 'the very last thing ... add this to a dashboard' and then says 'just as we did' while constructing an additional worksheet (869s), so omit that dependent setup. Use 877s at 'what I want to do ... show you how to combine those'; the two existing worksheet views are immediately explained as the objects to combine, and their earlier filter/color setup is not needed for understanding the dashboard action. At 883.88–905.32s the narrator selects New Dashboard, sets Automatic size and drops visualizations; at 905.32–927.32s he places/renames sheets and explains customization. This directly teaches f1/f2, not the new required worksheet-bar-chart fact f5, nor audience-specific sizing/arrangement. End before Bins at 931.36s. The concrete sheet/dashboard/drop-down/dragging cues establish screen-demo visual value. Pre-existing worksheets are visible inputs, not unexplained blocked knowledge.

Read 22–246s and Sharing Reports/Share Link/Manage Links chapters. At 53.04–81.68s a fresh published-report example selects Share, recipient and Send. At 136.8–160.48s link options and allow-reshare/allow-build permissions are named. At 163.12–214.96s the narrator deliberately chooses specific recipients and view-only access, applies it, sends the link and explains that only named people can view. This confirms f2/f3; the cut does not teach publishing or full license/capacity conditions. The original end is retained just before the manage-links workflow at 217.12s, after 'view the reports in it.' The preceding Pro-license simplification at 46–51s is outside the approved range. Choosing whether someone may build content does not require understanding the later semantic layer; it is presented as an optional permission rather than used as an unexplained calculation mechanism. Narrated Share dialogs, options and sent links provide screen-demo value.

Read 7–139s and What the CALCULATE function does/Data model and total sales with SUMX chapters. The 38.64s introduction restates the subject without relying on the earlier one-word analogy. At 43.88–78.83s monthly sales are shown with innovative-product/bulk filters added to the measure beyond the initial visual filter context; at 80.64–94.84s the narrator explicitly transfers the Excel pivot-table context to Power BI visuals. This supports f1's context-dependent measure model, although it is a specialized CALCULATE illustration rather than basic measure syntax, and no f2–f9 are confirmed. Stop before the rewind at 109.67s and SUMX/model setup at 119s. Pivot tables are already allowed; no Tableau calculation or semantic-layer knowledge is needed. Before/after sales views and filter references give meaningful visual cues, with frame-level layout unverified.

Read 55–352s and Create a Calculated Field/Local Calculated Fields chapters. At 86.8–166.2s the narrator opens the calculation editor by several routes, including Analysis > Create Calculated Field at 146.84–154.92s; at 167.72–178.32s he names a field, enters 1 and selects OK, confirming f2. The constant alone does not demonstrate deriving from source fields, but at 249.92–317.72s UPPER applied to customer first name changes the displayed value while re-adding the original field shows the source is unchanged, confirming f1. Extend to 322s so the sentence 'locally only available in this view' from 320.32–321.84s is finished before the reuse/promotion task. No Discount Ratio, row-versus-aggregate comparison or aggregation change is taught, so do not claim f3–f5. The earlier 65–76s cross-workbook-reuse claim is outside this cut; local/global here means view versus workbook availability, not a need to understand the blocked semantic layer. Editor/menu/field-icon and before/after view cues support visual value.

Read 148–376s and Datasets vs reports/Creating shared reports chapters. At 182.8–219s the narrator explicitly enumerates dataset/model contents: tables, source connection, transformations, relationships, calculated columns, measures and field formatting. At 236.88–282.96s he publishes a model and creates a new report connected to the existing dataset rather than its own. At 294.64–342.16s he saves a visualization and checks lineage, showing one dataset as the source of four reports. Confirm f1/f2; there is no shared measure definition (f3) or Build-permission requirement (full f4). Use 183s to start directly with the dataset definition; keep 345s at the completed four-reports point and exclude the subsequent thin-report repetition/Desktop workflow. 'Dataset' is legacy terminology for the semantic model and deserves a bridge note; it is not a different model object. Earlier data modeling and measures are allowed. The narrated service menu, saved report and lineage view provide concrete screen-demo cues.

Read 0–113s and What Are Build Permissions/How to Get Build Permissions chapters. Begin at 24s at the new Build-permission question, avoiding the preceding subscription sentence. At 28.38–47.13s shared datasets are explained as using a model in a workspace to create reports that may live in another workspace. At 47.13–58.44s creating a report from a shared dataset is explicitly tied to granting Build permission to a user/group. At 58.44–70.17s the point is avoiding data silos by reusing models across reports. This confirms f2/f4 as a conceptual connection/permission explanation, not a hands-on connection procedure or shared-measure definition. Tighten to 70s after the reuse point, excluding repetitive content-creation commentary and the next how-to question near 78s. The transcript only promises switching to the laptop at 80.79s, so this range likely has limited visuals. Approve under the talking-head exception: the concept is genuinely conceptual, and the short, explicit reuse/Build-permission explanation is exceptionally clear without an unseen diagram. No blocked knowledge remains at this final concept.
